content: A low sodium diet is defined as a dietary regimen that restricts sodium intake to no more than 1,500 to 2,400 milligrams per day. For reference, one teaspoon of salt contains approximately 2,300 milligrams of sodium. Individuals who engage in moderate to vigorous physical activity are generally advised to limit their sodium intake to 3,000 milligrams per day. Conversely, those with moderate to severe heart failure are typically recommended to restrict their sodium consumption to 2,000 milligrams per day. The minimum daily sodium requirement for human health is about 500 milligrams, which is significantly less—roughly one-sixth—than the sodium content found in many diets that are seasoned to taste. For individuals with salt-sensitive blood pressure, excessive sodium intake can have detrimental effects on health. A 2008 Cochrane review concluded that a long-term low sodium diet (lasting more than four weeks) in Caucasian populations effectively reduces blood pressure, both in individuals with hypertension and those with normal blood pressure. Previous Cochrane reviews have suggested that the impact of low versus high sodium intake on blood pressure may be more pronounced in Black and Asian populations compared to Caucasians. However, the number of studies involving Black and Asian participants in these reviews was insufficient to establish distinct recommendations for these groups. Sodium is naturally present in most foods, with sodium chloride (table salt) being the most common form. Foods such as milk, beets, and celery naturally contain sodium, as does drinking water, though the sodium content in water varies depending on its source. Sodium is also added to many food products in forms such as monosodium glutamate, sodium nitrite, sodium saccharin, baking soda (sodium bicarbonate), and sodium benzoate. These additives are commonly found in condiments and seasonings like Worcestershire sauce, soy sauce, onion salt, garlic salt, and bouillon cubes. Processed meats, including bacon, sausage, and ham, as well as canned soups and vegetables, are examples of foods with added sodium. Fast foods are generally very high in sodium, as are processed foods like potato chips, frozen dinners, and cured meats. Excessive salt levels in groundwater caused by regenerative water softeners have led to bans on these devices in over 60 cities in Southern California due to their impact on groundwater reclamation projects. Additionally, water labeled as drinking water in supermarkets may contain sodium, as it is often only filtered with carbon and retains any sodium present in the source water. Fresh, unprocessed foods such as fruits, vegetables, lean meats, poultry, fish, and unprocessed grains are naturally low in sodium. The availability of low sodium food options is increasing. However, finding low sodium versions of processed foods that are naturally high or moderately high in sodium—such as cereals, soups, and canned seafood—can be challenging. In response, food markets and distributors have begun establishing online businesses dedicated to marketing low sodium products. Similar to the rise of low-carb or low-calorie products, low sodium items are becoming a distinct category on food market shelves. Many low sodium products, such as low sodium soup bases, have transitioned from being exclusive to the hospitality industry to being widely available online.
